title: Exploring novel lead-free halide double perovskites X 2 LaCuBr 6  (X = Cs, Rb, K): stability, optoelectronic and thermoelectric properties – a first-principles study
content: Lead-free halide double-perovskites have the ability to meet the increasing demand for energy worldwide, making them attractive options for applications involving renewable energy. In the present work, we have investigated the structural, electronic, thermodynamic, optical, and thermoelectric properties of X2LaCuBr6 (X = Cs, Rb, K) using density functional theory (DFT). To demonstrate that the compounds under study are thermodynamically and structurally stable in the cubic phase, we calculated the Born stability criterion, cohesive energy (Ecoh), formation energy (ΔHf), phonon dynamics and Goldschmidt's tolerance factor (τ). Furthermore, the electronic properties were computed using the GGA + mBJ potentials. Applying the modified Becke–Johnson (mBJ) potential, the bandgap values of X2LaCuBr6 (X = Cs, Rb, and K) were determined as 1.77, 1.80, and 1.81 eV, respectively. Their applicability for high-frequency optoelectronic applications is indicated by the optical absorption spectra's low reflectivity and prominent absorption peaks in the UV and far-ultraviolet regions. The computed Seebeck coefficient values at 300 K are (Cs) 218.884 µV K−1, (Rb) 212.888 µV K−1, and (K) 207 µV K−1. The corresponding dimensionless thermoelectric figures of merit (zT) at 300 K for X2LaCuBr6 (X = Cs, Rb, K) are 0.33, 0.39, and 0.36 respectively. The obtained results give these materials attractive potential for possible use in thermoelectric devices. Furthermore, the calculated thermodynamic parameters, such as heat capacity, Debye temperature, thermal expansion coefficient, and entropy, exhibit predictable temperature and pressure-dependent behaviour. These properties, which demonstrate the compounds' thermodynamic stability, were calculated using the quasi-harmonic Debye model-based Gibbs2 software over a temperature range of 0–400 K and a pressure range of 0–2 GPa.
